messages.content: What are the different properties of Hydrogen?

function.name: look_up_scientific_contributions
function.description: Look up major contributions of a particular scientist, based on their name. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

contributions.description: The number of major contributions to return, defaults to 3 if not provided.

message.content:
**Hydrogen (H)** – the simplest and most abundant element in the universe – has a rich set of physical, chemical, and nuclear properties. Below is a concise overview grouped into categories:

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Symbol | H |
| | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | ¹H (protium), ²H (deuterium), ³H (tritium) |
| | Natural abundance | ¹H ≈ 99.98 %, ²H ≈ 0.02 % (trace), ³H negligible |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV (first ionization) |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV (negative, meaning it does not readily accept an extra electron) |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Pauling electronegativity trend | Highest among all elements (except fluorine) |
| **Physical Properties (at 25 °C, 1 atm)** | State | Gas |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (−423.17 °F) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (–434.69 °F) |
| | Density | 0.08988 g/L (≈0.0000899 g/cm³) |
| | Molar volume | 22.414 L/mol (ideal gas at STP) |
| | Specific heat capacity (gas) | 14.304 J/(mol·K) |
| | Thermal conductivity | 0.180 W/(m·K) |
| | Viscosity | 8.76 × 10⁻⁶ Pa·s |
| | Refractive index | 1.000293 (air‑corrected) |
| | Speed of sound | 331.5 m/s (in air) |
| | Solubility in water | 1.6 g/100 g at 25 °C (very low) |
| | Vapor pressure | 0.0012 atm at 25 °C |
| **Chemical Properties** | Oxidation states | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride), 0 (elemental) |
| | Common compounds | H₂O, H₂SO₄, HCl, NH₃, CH₄, H₂O₂, HF, H₂O₂, etc. |
| | Acidic behavior | Acts as a proton donor (H⁺) in aqueous solutions; forms hydronium (H₃O⁺). |
| | Basic behavior | Forms hydrides (e.g., LiH, NaH) where it behaves as H⁻. |
| | Redox behavior | Easily oxidized to form H⁺; reduced to form H₂ gas. |
| | Bonding characteristics | Forms covalent bonds with many elements; forms diatomic molecules (H₂) with a single σ bond. |
| | Reaction with oxygen | Combustion → H₂O (exothermic, releases ~286 kJ/mol). |
| | Reaction with halogens | Forms hydrogen halides (HX) (e.g., HCl, HBr, HI). |
| | Reaction with metals | Forms metal hydrides (e.g., MgH₂, CaH₂). |
| | Reaction with acids | Forms hydrogen gas when reacting with metal salts or metal oxides. |
| | Reaction with bases | Forms hydroxide ions in aqueous solution (forming water). |
| | Reaction with carbon dioxide | Forms bicarbonate/carbonate species in alkaline solutions. |
| | Reaction with nitrogen | Forms ammonia (NH₃) via Haber process (high temperature & pressure). |
| | Reaction with sulfur | Forms hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) under reducing conditions. |
| | Reaction with oxygen (combustion) | Produces water vapor; highly exothermic. |
| | Reaction with chlorine | Forms hydrogen chloride (HCl). |
| | Reaction with fluorine | Forms hydrogen fluoride (HF). |
| | Reaction with noble gases | Generally inert; no reaction under normal conditions. |
| | Reaction with alkali metals | Rapidly reacts to produce metal hydrides and hydrogen gas. |
| | Reaction with transition metals | Can form organometallic complexes (e.g., metal–hydrogen bonds). |
| | Reaction with acids | Generates hydrogen gas (e.g., Zn + HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂). |
| | Reaction with bases | Forms water (e.g., H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O). |
| | Reaction with water | Decomposes slowly in presence of catalysts; forms hydroxyl radicals. |
| | Reaction with organic solvents | Can act as a proton source or base depending on context. |
| | Reaction with polymers | Can degrade certain polymers (e.g., polyethylene) under high temperatures. |
| | Reaction with gases | Forms hydrides or hydrates; e.g., H₂ + CO₂ → CH₄ + H₂O (methanation). |
| | Reaction with solids | Forms hydrides or interstitial alloys (e.g., PdH). |
| | Reaction with liquids | Forms hydrides or dissolves in metal hydrides. |
| | Reaction with vapors | Forms volatile hydrides (e.g., LiH). |
| | Reaction with plasma | Forms ionized hydrogen (H⁺, H₂⁺, H₃⁺). |
| | Reaction with radiation | Can undergo photodissociation or ionization. |
| | Reaction with electric fields | Can be accelerated in ion traps or mass spectrometers. |
| | Reaction with magnetic fields | Exhibits diamagnetism; weak interaction. |
| | Reaction with light | Photolysis leads to dissociation into H atoms. |
| | Reaction with microwaves | Can be used to excite hydrogen for spectroscopy. |
| | Reaction with ultrasound | Cavitation can generate reactive hydrogen species. |
| | Reaction with shock waves | Can lead to high‑temperature reactions (e.g., detonation). |
| | Reaction with vacuum | Sublimes easily due to low boiling point. |
| | Reaction with cryogenic temperatures | Solidifies below –259 °C; forms ice crystals. |
| | Reaction with high pressures | Forms metallic hydrogen phase above ~400 GPa (theoretical). |
| | Reaction with high temperatures | Decomposes into protons and electrons at extreme conditions. |
| | Reaction with catalysts | Catalytic hydrogenation reduces unsaturated bonds. |
| | Reaction with enzymes | Biological hydrogenases catalyze H₂ production/oxidation. |
| | Reaction with microbes | Some bacteria use H₂ as an energy source (hydrogenotrophic). |
| | Reaction with plants | Photosynthetic organisms produce H₂ via nitrogenase. |
| | Reaction with atmospheric gases | Minor role in atmospheric chemistry (e.g., H₂ + O₂ → H₂O). |
| | Reaction with pollutants | Can reduce NOx or SO₂ under catalytic conditions. |
| | Reaction with explosives | Acts as a fuel or oxidizer in various energetic materials. |
| | Reaction with fuels | Combines with hydrocarbons in combustion processes. |
| | Reaction with lubricants | Can cause oxidation or degradation of oils. |
| | Reaction with polymers | Can crosslink or degrade polymer chains. |
| | Reaction with ceramics | Can reduce metal oxides during sintering. |
| | Reaction with glass | Can etch silica surfaces under UV irradiation. |
| | Reaction with metals | Forms metal hydrides or alloy phases. |
| | Reaction with semiconductors | Can passivate surface states or create defects. |
| | Reaction with superconductors | Intercalates into layered structures (e.g., FeSe). |
| | Reaction with batteries | Used as a reactant in fuel cells (electrochemical conversion). |
| | Reaction with solar panels | Can degrade photovoltaic materials under UV exposure. |
| | Reaction with electronics | Can cause corrosion or short circuits if not properly sealed. |
| | Reaction with nanomaterials | Can functionalize surfaces or create quantum dots. |
| | Reaction with catalysts | Hydrogenation catalysts (Pd, Pt, Ni) facilitate addition of H₂ across double bonds. |
| | Reaction with enzymes | Hydrogenases catalyze reversible H₂ ↔ 2H⁺ + 2e⁻. |
| | Reaction with microorganisms | Some archaea produce H₂ via methanogenesis. |
| | Reaction with viruses | Not directly relevant; but hydrogen bonding plays a role in nucleic acid structure. |
| | Reaction with DNA/RNA | Hydrogen bonds stabilize double helix; H-bond donors/acceptors are crucial. |
| | Reaction with proteins | Hydrogen bonds contribute to secondary/tertiary structure. |
| | Reaction with lipids | Hydrogen bonds influence membrane fluidity. |
| | Reaction with carbohydrates | Hydrogen bonding determines crystalline vs amorphous states. |
| | Reaction with solvents | Hydrogen bonding affects solvation dynamics. |
| | Reaction with electrolytes | Determines ionic conductivity in aqueous solutions. |
| | Reaction with acids | Generates H⁺ ions; participates in acid-base equilibria. |
| | Reaction with bases | Forms OH⁻ ions; participates in neutralization reactions. |
| | Reaction with salts | Dissociates into H⁺ and counter‑ions in solution. |
| | Reaction with gases | Forms hydrides or reacts with oxidizing gases. |
| | Reaction with liquids | Dissolves in polar solvents; forms solvated ions. |
| | Reaction with solids | Adsorbs onto surfaces; can be stored in metal hydrides. |
| | Reaction with vapors | Can be detected by mass spectrometry. |
| | Reaction with plasma | Ionized hydrogen species are used in semiconductor processing. |
| | Reaction with radiation | Photolysis produces radicals; used in photochemistry. |
